topic: 最弱项目补强与迁移复测
grammarFocus: 针对个人错误选择练习；每次订正后用新题检查，而不只重做旧题。
title: Week 51: Targeted Repair and Transfer Retest — The Riverside Repair Café
instructions: 本材料为模拟练习，不是官方雅思考试，也不对应任何官方分数。请先完成听力（四个部分，共40题），再完成阅读（三篇文章，共40题）。听力部分建议先读题再听录音（录音文字在 transcript 中，可先遮住）。所有填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。判断题只有 True / False / Not Given 三个选项；选 Not Given 时，请在解释中说明缺少哪个必要事实。完成后对照中文解释和原文证据进行订正；订正后请使用 grammar 和 transfer 部分的新题进行迁移复测，不要只重做旧题。
transcript:
SECTION 1: SOCIAL DIALOGUE

Receptionist: Good morning, Riverside Community Centre. How can I help?
Caller: Hi, I'm calling about the Repair Café that runs on Saturdays. A friend mentioned it, but I'm not sure how it works.
Receptionist: Of course. It's a monthly event where volunteers help people fix broken household items instead of throwing them away. We run it on the first Saturday of every month, from ten in the morning until two in the afternoon.
Caller: And it's free?
Receptionist: Entry is free, yes. But if a repair needs a spare part, you pay for the part itself. The volunteer labour is free.
Caller: That makes sense. What kind of things can people bring?
Receptionist: Small electrical items, bicycles, clothing, furniture, and toys. We don't accept anything with a cracked screen, though — phones and tablets are outside what our volunteers can safely repair.
Caller: Right. I've got a lamp that flickers and a wooden chair with a loose leg. Would those be suitable?
Receptionist: The lamp, definitely. The chair depends on the volunteer — we have a furniture repairer, but he only comes on alternate months. This month he's not here, so I'd suggest bringing the chair next month.
Caller: OK. Do I need to book?
Receptionist: You don't need to book for small items, but we do ask people to register large furniture in advance, because space is limited. For a lamp you can just turn up.
Caller: And how long does a repair usually take?
Receptionist: Between twenty minutes and an hour, depending on the queue. Saturdays are busy, so I'd arrive before eleven if you want to be seen quickly.
Caller: Is there anything I should bring with me?
Receptionist: If you have the instruction manual or any spare parts that came with the item, bring them. Also, please don't leave items unattended — you need to stay while the volunteer works, because they may ask you questions about how the fault started.
Caller: Understood. One more thing — can I bring my neighbour's kettle as well? She's elderly and can't come herself.
Receptionist: Yes, that's fine, as long as you can describe the problem. We only ask that each visitor brings a maximum of three items, so we can help everyone.
Caller: Great. And is there a café there? My friend said something about coffee.
Receptionist: There's a small refreshment table run by the youth group. Drinks are by donation — there's no fixed price. All the money goes towards buying tools.
Caller: Perfect. I'll come this Saturday with the lamp, then.
Receptionist: Lovely. Just sign in at the desk when you arrive, and take a numbered ticket.

SECTION 2: SOCIAL MONOLOGUE

Hello, and welcome to the Riverside Repair Café volunteer briefing. My name is Dana, and I coordinate the team. I want to explain how a typical Saturday works, so that new volunteers know what to expect.

We open the doors at ten, but volunteers arrive at half past nine. That half hour is for setting up tables, checking that the tool kits are complete, and reading the job sheet from the previous month. Please don't skip the briefing at twenty to ten — it's short, but it's where we mention any safety issues.

When visitors arrive, they sign in and receive a numbered ticket. The numbers are called in order, but we operate two queues: one for electrical items and one for everything else. This is because electrical repairs need a qualified volunteer at the table at all times, and we only have two people with that qualification.

Each repair has a time limit of forty-five minutes. If a job is clearly going to take longer, the volunteer should stop and explain the options to the visitor. Sometimes the honest answer is that the item cannot be repaired safely, and that is a perfectly good outcome. We are not here to promise success; we are here to give things a second chance.

A word about parts. We keep a box of common fuses, plugs, and screws, and these are free. Anything else — a special cable, a replacement motor — the visitor buys. Volunteers should never order parts without asking the coordinator first, because our budget is small and we need to keep records.

At the end of the day, we record every item on a simple form: what it was, whether it was repaired, and if not, why. This data matters. Last year we repaired sixty-eight per cent of the items brought in, and that figure helps us apply for funding. Please fill in the form before the visitor leaves, not afterwards, because details get forgotten.

Finally, a reminder about the space. The back room is for storage only. Please keep the walkway clear — last month someone tripped over a bicycle wheel, and although nobody was hurt, we must avoid a repeat. If you finish early, ask another volunteer if they need a hand rather than starting a new job yourself.

Thank you. Any questions, come and find me at the front desk.

SECTION 3: ACADEMIC DISCUSSION

Tutor: So, Mei, you've been looking at the repair café data for your project. What have you found?
Mei: Well, I started with the assumption that people come mainly to save money. But when I interviewed fifteen visitors, only four mentioned cost first. Most talked about not wanting to throw things away.
Tutor: That's interesting. So the environmental motive was stronger?
Mei: For the people I spoke to, yes. But I should be careful — fifteen people is a small sample, and they were all at one café.
Tutor: Good. That's exactly the kind of limitation you should state. Now, what about the repair success rate?
Mei: The café's own records say sixty-eight per cent last year. But I noticed the form only records whether the item worked when it left the café. It doesn't follow up a month later.
Tutor: So the figure measures something narrower than long-term repair.
Mei: Exactly. An item might work on Saturday and fail a week later. The sixty-eight per cent is really 'successful on the day'.
Tutor: How would you improve the data collection?
Mei: I'd suggest a short follow-up message after four weeks, asking one question: is the item still working? That would give a more meaningful figure without much extra effort.
Tutor: Reasonable. And what about the volunteers? Did you speak to them?
Mei: I did. Several said the most difficult part isn't the repair itself but explaining to visitors that something can't be fixed. One volunteer described it as 'managing disappointment'.
Tutor: That's a useful phrase. It suggests the volunteers need communication training, not just technical training.
Mei: Yes, and the briefing I observed focused almost entirely on tools and safety. There was nothing about how to say no.
Tutor: So your recommendation might be to add a short session on that.
Mei: I think so. Though I'd want to test it — maybe compare visitor satisfaction before and after.
Tutor: Good. Now, one more thing. You mentioned the two queues. Is that system working?
Mei: Mostly. But I noticed that the electrical queue moved much more slowly, and some visitors with electrical items left before their number was called.
Tutor: So the system may be discouraging exactly the people it was designed to help.
Mei: That's my reading, yes. I'd suggest giving electrical visitors an estimated waiting time when they arrive.
Tutor: Fine. Let's put that in your recommendations section. Remember to distinguish clearly between what you observed and what you infer.

SECTION 4: ACADEMIC LECTURE

Good afternoon. Today I want to discuss the concept of 'repair' as a form of learning, using community repair events as our example. This is a simulated case, but the principles are drawn from general educational research.

When we think about learning, we usually imagine a classroom, a teacher, and a curriculum. But a great deal of learning happens in what researchers call informal settings — places where nobody is officially a teacher and nobody is officially a student. The repair café is a good example. A visitor arrives with a broken lamp and a volunteer sits beside them. Who is teaching whom? The volunteer may know about wiring, but the visitor knows the history of the object: when it broke, how it was used, what has already been tried. The repair only succeeds if both kinds of knowledge are combined.

This has an important implication. In formal education, knowledge is often treated as something transferred from an expert to a novice. In informal settings, knowledge is more often negotiated. The volunteer does not simply announce the answer; they ask questions, test possibilities, and sometimes discover that their first idea was wrong. In other words, the expert is allowed to be uncertain in public. This is rare in classrooms, and it may be one reason why informal learning can feel less intimidating.

There is a second principle: the object itself constrains the learning. A lamp can only be repaired in certain ways. The physical object provides immediate feedback — either the light comes on or it does not. This kind of feedback is powerful because it is honest and instant. In academic subjects, feedback is often delayed and mediated by a teacher's judgement. The repair café offers a reminder that learning is often most effective when the learner can see the consequences of their actions.

A third principle concerns failure. In the repair café, roughly one item in three cannot be repaired. Volunteers are trained, at least in the better-run cafés, to treat this not as a personal failure but as a normal outcome. This attitude is worth examining. In many educational systems, failure is treated as a signal that the learner is not capable. But in repair, failure is information: it tells you what the object needs, or what you do not yet know. The difference is subtle but important. A learner who fears failure will avoid difficult tasks; a learner who reads failure as information will attempt them.

Finally, I want to mention transfer. Transfer means applying something learned in one situation to a new one. The repair café volunteer who fixes a lamp on Saturday may, on Monday, approach a broken office printer with more confidence. They have not learned about printers, but they have learned a general approach: observe, test, eliminate possibilities, ask for help. This is precisely what we hope for in education — not the memorisation of specific answers, but the ability to approach unfamiliar problems.

However, transfer is not automatic. Research suggests that transfer is more likely when learners are encouraged to reflect on what they did, rather than simply repeating the task. A volunteer who fixes ten lamps may become fast at fixing lamps, but may not become better at fixing anything else. A volunteer who, after each repair, is asked 'what principle did you use here?' is more likely to carry that principle to a new context. This is why reflection matters, and it is why, in your own studies, I ask you to explain your method and not only your answer.

So, to summarise: informal learning settings show us that expertise can be shared rather than transmitted, that objects can provide honest feedback, that failure can be read as information, and that transfer depends on reflection. These are not new ideas, but the repair café makes them visible.

grammar.title: 针对个人错误选择练习：用新题检查，而不是重做旧题
grammar.explanation: 很多学习者订正时只是把错题重做一遍，记住的是那道题的答案，而不是背后的规则。更有效的做法是：先找出自己错在哪一类（例如时态、介词、词形），然后换一个新句子、新语境来检查同一规则。下面四道题都是新句子，用来检查常见错误类型。
grammar.example: A volunteer who fixes ten lamps may become fast at fixing lamps, but may not become better at fixing anything else.

part1: Do you usually try to repair things yourself, or do you prefer to replace them?
Have you ever taken part in a community event like a repair café?
What kinds of skills do you think are most useful in everyday life?
Do you think schools should teach practical repair skills? Why or why not?
speaking.part2: Describe a time when you fixed something or learned a practical skill. You should say: what the object or skill was; why you needed to fix it or learn it; how you approached the problem; and how you felt about the result.
part3: Why do some people prefer to throw away broken items rather than repair them?
What role should communities play in reducing waste?
How can volunteers be trained to deal with difficult situations?
Do you think informal learning is as valuable as formal education?

transfer.writing: You have read about a community repair café. Write a short report (about 200 words) for a local community group recommending whether to start a similar project. In your report, describe the main benefits, mention one possible difficulty, and make a recommendation. Use your own ideas and do not copy sentences from the reading or listening.
